title: The problem with "parity of esteem"
author: Christodoulou, Daisy
summary: Daisy Christodoulou argues that vocational qualifications like The Knowledge and City & Guilds are often more rigorous than university degrees—but the UK government's proposal to introduce vocational options at age 14 is structurally unworkable. Comprehensive secondary schools lack the specialist equipment, industry partnerships, and practitioner expertise needed to deliver high-quality vocational training. Treating vocational courses as alternatives for lower-attaining students also undermines the very qualifications that carry real labour market value.
points: Vocational qualifications like The Knowledge and City & Guilds provide real status, self-worth, and earning power—often more rigorous than university degrees, not less.
"Parity of esteem" policies backfire when vocational courses function as academic exit routes for struggling students, stigmatising the qualifications and eroding their market value.
High-quality vocational training requires specialist facilities, real workplaces, and expert practitioners that comprehensive secondary schools structurally cannot provide.
Evidence from 2000s vocational-at-14 experiments shows the courses generated low-level qualifications worth a fraction of their stated GCSE equivalents, discrediting the entire approach.
Genuine reform would require 14-19 FE colleges operating at scale—a structural change the current English school system does not have in place.
quotes: So the problem is that if you do see vocational courses as being an alternative for students with low academic attainment, it will often make it harder to run the kinds of vocational courses that have the greatest labour market value.

I think they are better thought of as foundational qualifications that provide students with skills and knowledge that help them understand the world and that provide the basis for more advanced academic and vocational study.

The only way I think you could make vocational at 14 work at scale is if you completely restructured our system so that everyone took their GCSEs aged 14, secondary schools became 11-14, and FE colleges expanded to 14-19.

There is a world of difference between what you can achieve by taking a City & Guilds or a degree apprenticeship or The Knowledge, and what it is possible to do in our current school system at ages 14 to 16.

There are a number of specific structural reasons that make it really hard to deliver high-quality vocational training at scale in comprehensive schools to 14-year-olds, and I will explain them later.
